data.title: Issue 221: COP31 goes big on carbon markets; South-east Asia enhances Asean Power Grid agreement
data.description:
Carbon markets

Policy, aggregation lead carbon approaches at COP31

Public-sector support and market aggregation have emerged as two major areas of focus for carbon markets at the annual United Nations climate conference in Turkey.

South-east Asia, with its rich and abundant ecosystems, stands to gain if governments are able to catalyse improved confidence and scale in carbon markets.

The hosts of the climate meeting, known as COP31, had identified carbon markets as a priority issue to better channel capital towards activities that positively impact climate change.

Over the past week, 17 governments endorsed a “policy playbook” that describes eight levers that policymakers can use to enable carbon credit markets at “speed and scale”. The playbook is authored by the Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets, a group of 18 governments – including Canada, Indonesia, the Philippines, Singapore and Britain – working to unlock corporate demand for high-integrity carbon credits.

The playbook has a noticeably practical bent, with the policy levers going beyond broad principles to policy actions for countries to implement. The eight levers themselves serve three policy objectives:

  • Support corporate purchases of high-integrity carbon credits;
  • Build buyer confidence and mitigate risk; and
  • Support the development of effective carbon credit markets.

Singapore has also been active on the carbon markets front at COP31.

A Singapore-World Bank partnership known as the Singapore Carbon Markets for Development Programme has released a three-year work plan aimed at helping developing countries to build infrastructure and capabilities to take part in carbon markets.

Singapore authorised the first project aligned with international rules that govern cross-border trading of carbon credits, a clean-water initiative in Rwanda. Preliminary carbon credit deals have also been secured with Kenya and Colombia.

The policy playbook, the cross-border carbon deals and government-driven carbon market initiatives reflect growing government involvement in carbon markets as countries and industries pursue decarbonisation targets, and could provide important tailwinds if supportive policies are put in place.

Another piece of the carbon market puzzle is scale, and aggregation appears to be a favoured solution of the moment.

A Singapore-initiated public-private group called the Action for a Resilient Climate (ARC) coalition – which aims to raise corporate demand for carbon credits – plans to launch its first tender in 2027 to buy a million tonnes of credits.

The policy playbook explains the logic of aggregation. The hypothesis is that pooling demand reduces due diligence costs, supports market building and proofs of concept, and improves the financeability of projects through long-term offtake agreements. Buyers benefit because they can spread risk, improve access and standardise risk management.

Aggregation is being applied on the supply side as well, with project aggregation among the approaches being explored by the Singapore-World Bank programme.

The focus on carbon markets bodes well for South-east Asia, as does the fact that Indonesia, the Philippines and Singapore are part of The Coalition to Grow Carbon Markets. The region continues to face a sizable climate investment gap, which thriving carbon markets can help to close. One estimate by Singapore bank DBS places the region’s cumulative climate investment requirement at US$5.2 trillion from 2025 to 2035 across mitigation, adaptation and resilience areas.

EY notes that South-east Asia accounts for about 30 per cent of the world’s nature-based solutions potential, and has the world’s largest “blue carbon” storage capacity largely due to mangrove areas. Blue carbon projects, in particular, also offer substantial biodiversity benefits. The consultancy estimates that nature-based solutions projects have delivered internal rates of return between 2 and 12 per cent.

A 2025 green-economy report by Bain & Co, GenZero, Google, Standard Chartered and Temasek estimates that South-east Asia’s six largest economies issued about 20 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent credits in 2024, far short of the roughly 720 million tonnes of annual credits from nature-based solutions in those countries.

Singapore, in particular, could potentially reap many benefits. Being an urban, natural resource-limited country, Singapore needs to rely on carbon credits as it progresses towards its climate goals. Furthermore, Singapore has a strategic ambition to be a sustainable finance hub, and thriving carbon markets would be important validation for those plans.

Energy transition

Asean Power Grid is more than a bunch of bilateral deals

South-east Asian leaders have signed an enhanced memorandum of understanding (MOU) on the Asean Power Grid (APG), a regionwide electricity network that was first conceived in 1997 but has made little progress in the 30 years since.

Asean covers 11 countries with very different energy profiles across a vast expanse of land and water, hence difficulty in building a regional power network amid such complexity should not be surprising.

In recent years, Singapore’s pursuit of low-carbon energy imports from its neighbours has fuelled optimism that such imports can spark faster progress on the APG. However, there is a limit to how much Singapore’s energy import projects can advance the APG, because there are fundamental differences between the mostly bilateral, one-way import deals that Singapore is trying to set up and the multilateral, two-way interconnections embodied in the APG’s vision of supporting regional energy resilience.

Some of that complexity is explained in the International Energy Agency’s study into financing the APG. A key observation in the report is that most of the investments in cross-border power projects in South-east Asia have been for one-way power exports, but such investments are insufficient to meet the needs of bi-directional, grid-to-grid projects required by the APG.

Among the APG’s goals are to allow South-east Asian countries to harness complementary energy resources. The Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ announcement about the latest MOU states that the APG can help to “diversify electricity supplies, improve power system resilience and support renewable energy integration”.

A fee framework that governs how much Singapore will pay for electricity from Indonesia is very different from a two-way agreement that would allow Indonesia to buy electricity from Singapore, much less rules that determine how 11 different countries can trade electricity among themselves. There are also questions involving how capital and operating expenditures related to infrastructure and running the networks should be split, with such decisions taking on a substantially different level of complexity in a multilateral arrangement versus a bilateral one.

The point is that while bilateral deals can help to move progress on the APG forward in certain areas, Asean cannot escape the need to establish a common set of fundamental arrangements across the region as a whole. It will certainly be complicated and challenging, but the struggle will almost certainly be worth it when considering the benefits that a deal could unlock.

  • PM Wong pitches deeper Asean ties on digital payments, energy and haze
  • Malaysia loosens rare earths curbs for France amid upgrade of ties to strategic partnership
  • China’s fossil fuel power tips towards annual drop on green boom
  • Why Singapore should stop trying to recycle everything

data.title: Singapore stocks fall in tandem with regional downturn; STI down 2.1%
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Singapore stocks ended lower on Friday (Nov 20) in tandem with regional declines, tracking overnight losses on Wall Street as Anthropic’s debut on Nasdaq failed to lift the broader market.

The Straits Times Index (STI) lost 2.1 per cent or 104.32 points to finish at 4,975.17. Twenty-six of the benchmark index’s 30 constituents ended the day lower; the remaining four closed flat.

Alvin Lee, premium client manager at IG, said the movement “mirrors the overall risk off sentiment we are seeing across major indices even outside the US, such as the Nikkei and Kospi, which are both down more than 5 per cent”.

“The risk-off sentiment has come from concerns over a hawkish Fed that is widely expected to raise rates even further, with markets pricing in an almost absolute certainty of a rate hike of 25 basis points in December,” he added.

The worst performer among STI constituents was Seatrium , which fell 8.8 per cent or S$0.15 to S$1.56.

CGS International previously downgraded its target price on the counter, a move that Lee said “did no favours to Seatrium’s share price” after a “bearish US session which spread into the STI in general”.

Separately, Seatrium said on Thursday that it expects its FY2026 underlying net profit to be “materially higher” than for FY2025.

The local banks all ended lower on Friday. DBS lost 1.8 per cent or S$1.23 to S$66.11, OCBC fell 3.2 per cent or S$0.88 to S$26.54, and UOB was down 2 per cent or S$0.72 at S$35.42.

Across the broader market, losers beat 493 to 163, after 1.4 billion securities worth S$2.6 billion changed hands.

Key regional indices also ended the day lower.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index lost 1.9 per cent, Japan’s Nikkei 225 fell 5.1 per cent, South Korea’s Kospi was down 5.2 per cent and the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI declined 0.6 per cent.

This article was written with the assistance of AI and reviewed by a reporter

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: Mistral AI opens regional HQ in Singapore, seeks to fill 200 roles in Apac
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] French artificial intelligence firm Mistral AI opened its Asia-Pacific headquarters in Singapore on Friday (Nov 20), to host most of the 200 staff that it plans to have in the region by 2027.

The company had around 40 staff in Singapore in May, when CEO Arthur Mensch told The Business Times that it was planning for 100 employees by the end of the year.

Geoff Soon, vice-president of revenue for the Asia-Pacific at Mistral, told BT that Singapore is “not a sales and marketing team”.

“I would say it is about 70 per cent forward deployment capabilities,” he said, pointing out that the company will hire a mix of forward deployment engineers and scientists to fill the Singapore headcount.

He added that Mistral will be looking to hire talents from “leading universities” for these roles.

Forward deployment – a term that has recently gathered pace due to the rise of AI – is the practice of allowing engineers to directly communicate with customers.

Soon said that unlike other tech firms, where engineers typically only fine-tune AI models, the individuals that Mistral recruits will be directly involved in development. “Scientists do the models, the engineers do the agentic capability,” he explained.

Talent is one of the reasons the company set up its regional headquarters in Singapore. Soon noted that the Republic has hosted several multinational manufacturing firms for a long period, giving Mistral an existing talent pool to draw from.

However, he acknowledged that the company will also need to tap people from outside Singapore for roles that workers here cannot fill.

The company will therefore seek to hire an even split of local and international talents. Soon noted that, to this end, Singapore “offers an amazing culture”, which will make it easier to convince people to relocate here.

Speaking as the guest of honour at the opening of Mistral’s office at Asia Square Tower, Senior Minister of State for Digital Development and Information Tan Kiat How said that having a presence in Singapore is not just about the physical office or headcount.

“It is the capability that grows around it,” he noted, adding that capability can be raised through researchers working on harder problems and engineers gaining exposure and experience with frontier AI models.

Targeting regulated industries

Mistral develops open-source and open-weight large language models. This means that the AI models can run locally on-premises, within company servers, allowing for greater sovereignty and security.

Soon said that the company will, building on its strengths, focus on serving regulated industries such as financial services and the public sector.

Mistral already has a presence in Singapore through partnerships with the Home Team Science and Technology Agency, as well as DSO National Laboratories. The company also has “other customers that are very focused on creating custom models to deliver their sovereign capabilities”.

Asked about his biggest concern about Mistral’s expansion plans, Soon said that more investments need to be made in the digital infrastructure layer. This includes access to more compute such as data centres and chips.

“We need lots of infrastructure,” he added, “to run our experiments and to develop new capabilities as we start to move into longer running agents.”

data.title: Soilbuild lawsuit: Brookfield says it moved ahead amid pressure to close S$535.3 million Mapletree deal
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Brookfield Asset Management, accused by Singapore billionaire Lim Chap Huat’s Soilbuild Group of “usurping” a joint venture (JV) deal, expanded on its defence arguments saying it faced “consistent commercial pressure” to close the deal with Mapletree Industrial Trust (MIT).

Lim and Soilbuild had alleged in an action filed on Aug 3 that Brookfield agreed to pursue the acquisition through a JV, and that the two sides worked together for several months on the proposed deal. They claim that Brookfield pulled out of the tie-up two days before Mapletree announced the S$535.3 million sale of the properties to the US asset manager.

In an Oct 20 response to a request for more detail on Brookfield’s defence, the asset manager said: “Mapletree was pressing Brookfield to complete the acquisition of the final seed assets as soon as possible, including by communicating the intended timing for completion and the difficulties in extending Brookfield’s exclusivity period.”

The final seed assets were The Strategy, The Synergy and Woodlands Central. The Strategy replaced 18 Tai Seng in the initial portfolio.

Brookfield gave the account in further particulars of its defence dated Oct 20 seen by The Business Times. The document was served in response to an Oct 6 request for more detail on Brookfield’s defence, including the commercial pressure it said it faced.

It had earlier maintained that it faced “consistent commercial pressures (including from Mapletree) to move ahead with the acquisition expeditiously” so as to maintain the credibility of the interest it had expressed in its letter of intent dated Feb 11, 2025.

In its defence dated Aug 31, Brookfield also said that, despite several rounds of negotiations, “the parties remained in disagreement on multiple key issues” that it considered could not reasonably be resolved. It added that it was “commercially impractical” to delay the purchase indefinitely while awaiting an agreement on the proposed JV.

The US investment giant said its Singapore arm offered S$535.3 million to Mapletree for the revised portfolio in the non-binding letter of intent on Feb 11, 2025.

Brookfield said Mapletree told it on Apr 21, 2025, that it had originally intended the acquisition to take place on May 2, 2025, and was facing “significant pushback” over extending Brookfield’s exclusivity period to May 8, 2025.

It added that Mapletree told it on May 8 that “the acquisition documentation should be finalised as soon as possible”.

On May 15, 2025, Mapletree inquired about the status of the acquisition, and asked whether Brookfield was ready to execute the acquisition documentation that same day, said Brookfield.

“There was also a focus on completing the acquisition of the final seed assets expeditiously including during weekly progress meetings, where Brookfield and other participants in the weekly progress meetings were reminded regularly of the impending expiration of its exclusivity period, and the acquisition timelines,” Brookfield noted.

It told Soilbuild on May 14 that it would proceed with the acquisition on its own.

On May 16, 2025, MIT’s manager announced that sale agreements had been signed for the three properties with buyers managed by Brookfield affiliates. The sale was completed on Aug 15, 2025.

Soilbuild’s claims and Brookfield’s defence 

Brookfield, its Singapore arm and a Brookfield-controlled entity are named defendants in the lawsuit filed with Singapore’s High Court, while Soilbuild’s executive chairman Lim, Soilbuild and a Soilbuild unit are named as claimants.

Lim and Soilbuild are seeking unspecified damages over Brookfield’s alleged breach of an agreement to pursue the JV, as well as the alleged unauthorised use of Soilbuild’s proprietary commercial information, among other claims.

Brookfield denies that the parties had entered into a JV, and said the opportunity to acquire the properties from Mapletree originated from Brookfield. Its Singapore arm submitted its first non-binding offer on Dec 5, 2024, before Brookfield was introduced to the Soilbuild team on Dec 18, it said.

The asset manager added that its Singapore arm and Soilbuild subsequently signed two confidentiality agreements for the initial and revised portfolios.

According to Brookfield, both agreements provided that neither party had “any legally binding obligations to negotiate or consummate the transaction” and that either party could “notify the other party in writing at any time to terminate discussions relating to the transaction”.

It also denied that the parties had agreed on or entered into a memorandum of understanding and that it wrongfully used Soilbuild’s alleged confidential information.

It also denied Soilbuild’s claim that it could not have completed the acquisition without the property group’s involvement.

Including the partial sale at TBTG’s initial public offering last year, the investment returned about S$70 million in cash to Thakral. The group plans to use the latest proceeds for new investments, its existing businesses and other capital needs. Shares of Thakral ended flat at S$1.45 on Thursday, before the announcement.

Katrina Group : An entity linked to carmaker BYD raised its stake in the F&B operator to 13.09 per cent from 4.91 per cent after buying more than 21 million shares for S$500,000 in an off-market transaction. It became a substantial shareholder in September, when it acquired a 5 per cent stake by buying 12.6 million shares from Katrina’s CEO for S$299,880. Shares of Katrina ended 8.3 per cent or S$0.003 higher at S$0.039 on Thursday, before the news.

data.title: Four fiery football friendly fixtures that kept the fans wanting more
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Four pulsating football matches. Twenty goals that bulged the back of the net. More than 72,000 fans passing through the turnstiles.

The inaugural Mizuho Blue Challenge: The Kallang Football Series – a quadrangular event featuring five-time World Cup champions Brazil, Asia’s top-ranked team Japan, South American side Paraguay and the Singapore Lions – delivered on most counts.

The 31st-ranked Paraguay, which reached the Round of 16 at this year’s Fifa World Cup, were impressive as they swept Singapore aside 4-1 in the opening contest on Friday (Nov 13) evening.

Japan and Brazil dazzled the crowd the next day as the Samurai Blue – backed by thousands of vociferous supporters in the stands – scored an injury-time goal to seal a breathtaking 3-2 victory.

And on Tuesday, a relentless Brazil netted seven without reply against Singapore. About an hour after that match wrapped up, Paraguay showed their might as they defeated Japan 2-1 in what was head coach Hajime Moriyasu’s final game in charge.

BT Weekend was at the National Stadium for all four fixtures and here are some takeaways from what was a memorable international festival of football.

Just a kickabout? Far from it

Anyone who turned up at the venue (or tuned in from home) expecting these teams to play at half-pace, simply because these were friendly games, received a pleasant surprise.

The four teams were competitive and serious from the first whistle and there was plenty of intensity from the players and coaching staff. What really captivated the crowd was that desire to go all out to get the victory and put on a solid performance – even though there were no trophies to be won.

It was quite a surprise to see Brazil striker Vinicius Jr play the full 90 minutes against Japan, and then turn up three days later to put in a 70-minute shift against Singapore. The Real Madrid star bagged five goals in total, making him the Mizuho Blue Challenge’s top scorer.

The Paraguay squad clocked a lot of air miles to make it to Singapore, and they made sure to make the most of their stay in the Lion City. They scored a total of six goals in two impressive wins over Singapore and Japan, with the likes of Miguel Almiron and Gustavo Gomez leading the way.

Jerseys galore

Of all the fans that thronged The Kallang on the three match days, a good number of them were decked out in the jerseys of the participating teams.

The merchandise stand at OCBC Square outside the Kallang Wave Mall was doing a roaring trade for hours as snaking queues formed to snap up S$59 event T-shirts and other memorabilia, as well as official jerseys that cost well over 100 dollars and much more if they were personalised with a player’s name and squad number.

The Japanese supporters turned up in droves to watch their side in action, and many of them wore the famous blue “home” jersey and the now sold-out off-white “away” shirt. Arguably the most popular last name on the back of those jerseys was midfielder Takefusa Kubo, who had the crowd on their feet when he scored the opening goal in the win over Brazil. Brazil’s signature yellow shirt was a common sight too, with those bearing players’ names such as Neymar, Ronaldo and Vinicius Jr among the more popular ones.

Steep learning curve for the Lions

Maybe it was a bit of a blessing in disguise that next year’s Asian Cup was pushed back by 11 months to the end of 2027, rather than take place in January.

That will give the Singapore players and coach Gavin Lee more time to prepare for the tournament in Saudi Arabia, and to get more exposure and games against other teams in the region and beyond.

The Lions have endured a rather torrid run of results of late, having lost four of their last five games in the last couple of months. They fell 0-6 to Causeway rivals Malaysia and failed to progress past the group stage of the Fifa Asean Cup in October. At the Mizuho Blue Challenge, Lee watched his players struggle to keep up with Paraguay and Brazil, letting in 11 goals in those two games alone.

Still, the Lions showed plenty of heart and fighting spirit and with more than a year to go until the Asian Cup, they should be in much better shape to face their group stage opponents Australia, Iraq and Tajikistan.

data.title: Working on my own terms
data.description:
AT 76, I still look forward to having something meaningful to do each day.

My golden years give me greater freedom to choose how I spend my time, be it by contributing through work, sharing what I have learnt, serving the community or enjoying the people and pursuits that enrich my life.

Recently, my Raffles Institution cohort celebrated the 60 years since completing our O levels in 1966. Many schoolmates have retired and are enjoying travel, family life and community service.

I am among the few who continue to work. Our paths differ, but we all face a worthwhile question: How do we make these years fulfilling?

A fulfilling life need not include paid work, a board appointment or a crowded diary. It can be found in caring for family, pursuing a new hobby, joining a community group or being a dependable mentor.

What matters is that the individual remains interested in life and connected to others.

Work with a different purpose

At this stage, work is less about earning money and more about engaging my mind and putting my experience to good use.

Board discussions and advisory assignments require me to listen carefully, question assumptions and consider unfamiliar problems. They are a form of mental gymnastics I enjoy, and I hope such stimulating intellectual challenges will keep dementia at bay.

My corporate roles also connect me with people across countries, industries and generations. Experience gives me a perspective to offer, though I do not assume to have all the answers. Younger colleagues often help me see fresh possibilities.

Having spent more than 30 years as a CEO, technopreneur and private investor, including my tenure as vice-president and managing director for the Asia-Pacific at Compaq, I have helped businesses with listings, mergers, accelerated growth and turnarounds.

These experiences have value beyond the positions I once held. The lessons learnt from difficult decisions, mistakes and setbacks can help others navigate their own challenges. Our usefulness does not end when our formal careers do.

Share what experience has taught us

Teaching entrepreneurship and leadership at the National University of Singapore, alongside mentoring members of the Singapore Institute of Directors and other professional networks, have allowed me to pass on some of these lessons. Knowledge accumulated over five decades should be passed on.

Mentoring is a rewarding way for seniors to contribute, and it need not happen through a formal programme. We can help a young colleague think through a career decision or encourage someone recovering from a setback. Sometimes, attentive listening is more useful than advice.

Learning also flows both ways. Younger people bring fresh perspectives and introduce unfamiliar technologies. Seniors should remain willing to learn and ask for help.

Find fulfilment in service

Public and community service have brought me deep fulfilment.

Through my mediation work with the State Courts and community centres, I have helped people resolve disputes in business and with family and neighbours.

When parties reach a settlement, I feel privileged to have helped them find a way forward – a reminder to be grateful for the peace in my own life.

I also served as a Justice of the Peace for 15 years and continue to solemnise marriages. Helping couples begin their journey together is a joy; it gives me an opportunity to share advice drawn from my former leadership roles at the National Family Council and the Centre for Fathering.

Service is open to all of us. A senior need not chair an organisation to make a difference. Reading with a child, visiting someone who lives alone or calling a withdrawn friend can be a meaningful contribution. We can all give the gift of time.

Discover new interests

Writing has enabled me to turn reflections into something useful to others. I have authored six books – including Golden Nuggets, an anthology of stories by seniors – which have collectively raised more than S$3 million for charities.

But we do not need to publish a book to preserve our stories; recording these tales or sharing memories with grandchildren leaves a precious inheritance.

Another source of pleasure is birding, which I took up five years ago after a slipped disc led me to give up golf. It has brought me to local spots like Kranji Marshes and overseas locations in search of unfamiliar species.

My camera now accompanies me on business trips to cities from London to Shanghai, and I go birding whenever time permits.

Birding has taught me to slow down and enjoy discovery. For other seniors, that delight may come from painting, cooking or learning about artificial intelligence.

We are never obliged to remain the people our careers required us to be.

Plan for the next chapter

Staying active requires judgment. Health, mobility and finances differ. During illness or recovery, participation may take a quieter form: a telephone conversation, reading or light activity with a friend.

Accepting help can make continued engagement possible.

We must also be willing to let go of roles that no longer fit. Saying “yes” to purpose sometimes requires saying “no” to more activity, ensuring we make time for relationships that are central to the lives we enjoy. Making time for my wife, children, children-in-law and grandchildren is as worthwhile as any professional achievement.

Earlier as an engineering student, I developed a life plan with three stages.

In Plan A, I would work for others and for money. In my current Plan B, I let others and money work for me, giving me greater freedom to choose my contributions.

In Plan C, which I intend to move towards at 80, I hope to devote more time to two areas spelled with a capital “C” – Church and Charity – and less to the smaller “c” – corporate commitments – while retaining selected engagements where I can be useful.

Crucially, the plan can evolve. Its value is that it encourages me to think deliberately about how I want to live.

The average lifespan of a Singaporean man is 84 years. Theoretically, I have eight more years to live, but that is not a given. I prefer to treat that uncertainty as a reason to appreciate today.

For seniors wondering where to begin, choose one manageable step: contact a friend, explore a hobby, learn something unfamiliar or offer an hour of help. Each is a reason to look forward to tomorrow.

I share my journey to encourage active, joyful ageing. There is still much to enjoy, discover and contribute. “No time” should never be an excuse to pursue a worthwhile purpose.

If I can have a vertical take-off from the short runway ahead of me, I will seize it to enjoy my life to the fullest.

For these reasons, retirement is not in my vocabulary.

The writer is the former vice-president and managing director of Compaq Computer Asia-Pacific. He is also a board member, senior advisor, adjunct professor and mediator.
